title: Queues and linked structures
summary: Implement a bounded ring buffer with constant-time enqueue and dequeue, and reason about linked pointers and iterator invalidation.

scenario.briefing: The render farm feeds frames to workers through a fixed-capacity queue. The current queue calls Array.shift on every dequeue, which copies every remaining frame, and enqueue uses push, so the array grows past its capacity. Replace the representation with a ring buffer that wraps its indexes, tracks its own count, and rejects overflow.

objectives.description: Apply the taught syntax in a working file.

hints: Compute the tail as (head + count) % capacity before writing.
Reject enqueue when count equals capacity; do not grow the array.
Read the head slot, clear it, then advance head with modulo.
Return the stored count from the getter so size stays O(1).

misconceptions.feedback: shift copies every remaining element down one index. A ring buffer moves an index instead.

misconceptions.description: Writing at head + count without wrapping.
misconceptions.feedback: Once the tail passes the last slot it must wrap to the front. Use modulo capacity.

misconceptions.description: Removing nodes while an iterator holds a pointer into the list.
misconceptions.feedback: The iterator's next pointer can skip or revisit nodes. Snapshot the values or invalidate the iterator on mutation.

sections.title: A ring buffer reuses fixed slots
sections.body: A circular queue keeps an array of capacity slots, a head index, and a count. The tail is (head + count) % capacity, so enqueue writes one slot and dequeue reads one slot. Both operations update two integers and never move the remaining values.

sections.title: A linked list moves pointers, not elements
sections.body: A singly linked list stores a value and a next reference per node. With a head and a tail pointer, appending at the tail and removing at the head are O(1). Finding or removing an arbitrary node still requires a walk, so the cost depends on which operation the structure promises.

sections.title: Pointer discipline prevents lost nodes
sections.body: Before reassigning a next pointer, keep the node you still need. A missing null check can dereference the end of the list, and a stale tail pointer can turn an O(1) append into a full walk. A sentinel node removes the empty-list special case.

sections.title: Mutation invalidates iterators
sections.body: An iterator stores a node reference or an index. If the queue changes during traversal, that position can skip an element, repeat one, or point at a removed node. Snapshot the values or make the iterator fail when the structure changes.

steps.title: Implement a bounded ring-buffer queue
steps.prompt: Edit structures.ts. Store values in a fixed array of slots. Enqueue at (head + count) % capacity and reject a full queue. Dequeue from head, clear the slot, and advance head with modulo. Keep size as the stored count.

tests.description: The queue keeps its generic shape and validates the capacity.
Enqueue writes at the wrapped tail and increments the count.
Dequeue reads the head, clears the slot, and advances with modulo.
Size returns the stored count instead of scanning the slots.

steps.title: Queue invariants and pointer costs

statements.label: A ring buffer advances its head with modulo instead of shifting every remaining element.
Array.shift removes the first element in constant time.
A singly linked list with a maintained tail pointer can append in O(1).
An iterator over a linked list stays valid after the node it points at is removed.
A ring buffer needs a stored count because the backing array length stays at capacity.

steps.explanation: The ring buffer makes dequeue constant time by moving an index and clearing the vacated slot. A linked list can match that cost when it keeps both ends, but arbitrary access and deletion require a walk. Mutation invalidates iterators because their stored position no longer describes the same element.
